title: Learning Strategy: Think Like a Runner
author: Stuart Jr., Dave
summary: Stuart uses a thought experiment about two runners with the same 20 training hours to argue that students should spread study out instead of cramming. Runner A trains a little each day and rests before the race, while Runner B packs all her hours into the final week. He observes that Runner A arrives fresh and fit, and that students prepare their brains for assessments and essays the way Runner B prepares her legs. He admits he has not mastered teaching this habit but is motivated by Cal Newport's study of top university students, who think like runners. He extends the point to wellbeing, noting that Runner A also avoids the nagging sense of procrastination and the miserable final week. The piece concludes that the strategy makes students saner as well as better at school, and credits Barbara Oakley for a similar analogy.
points: Distributed practice beats last-minute cramming even when the crammer uses more total hours.
The running analogy gives students an intuitive, physical model for why the brain cannot be crammed.
Newport's high-achieving students are offered as evidence that working smarter, not harder, is teachable to ordinary ninth graders.
Spreading work out also reduces the stress and dread that accompany procrastination.
quotes: Runner A practices for 30 minutes per day, 6 days a week. She doesn't practice at all the 2 days just before the race, either. All told, she spends about 75% of her allotted training hours.
The answer, of course, is Runner A because you can't cram for a race. Even though she didn't use her 20 practice hours, she's in way better running shape on race day than Runner B.

While most students would find this a silly story, it's exactly the way that they attempt to prepare another part of their body — their brain — for big assessments, and it's also the way they attempt to get their brains to produce longer essays. Last-minute work, unfortunately, is about as smart in the realm of the brain as it is in the realm of the lungs and legs. My students, and probably yours, could certainly benefit to think more like a runner.

In the book, Newport describes how the types of students he studies — those who achieve top-level success at top-level universities, all while maintaining balanced lives — think like runners when it comes to preparing for exams or writing large essays. If it's something that helps Ivy League kids work smarter not harder, then it's something I want to try teaching my small-town ninth graders to try.

Afterward, though, she did whatever else she had to do without any nagging sense of putting things off. Runner B, on the other hand, did have the nagging sense, and she also had a pretty miserable week prior to race day, putting in grueling practices for several hours a day, 7 days in a row.
